q: Calculate the percentage increase in person A’s glucose in the first 30 minutes.
Explain the change in person A’s glucose from 30 to 120 minutes.
Beta cells in the pancreas detect the high glucose and release insulin; liver and muscle cells take up glucose and store it as glycogen, so the level returns to normal.
Use the rules above the graph to classify persons B and C.
B: diabetes (fasting 7.4, and 11.9 at 120 min). C: prediabetes (8.6 at 120 min).
Suggest two reasons why person B’s glucose stays high.
Any two: body cells do not respond to insulin (type 2); the pancreas makes too little insulin; fewer glucose transporters move into cell membranes.
Suggest why the test is done after an overnight fast.
Recent food would raise glucose and change the starting level; fasting gives a standard baseline, so people can be compared fairly.

22.t: Working with data: a cold room
q: Compare the change in core and skin temperature over 60 minutes.
Core temperature fell only 0.3 °C; skin temperature fell 13 °C.
Explain why skin temperature fell so much.
Vasoconstriction: arterioles supplying the skin narrow, so less warm blood reaches the surface and the skin cools towards room temperature.
Oxygen use more than doubled. Explain how this helped keep core temperature steady.
Shivering: rapid muscle contractions need more ATP, so respiration speeds up; respiration releases heat, replacing heat lost to the room.
Explain why a cold skin reduces heat loss.
Heat loss depends on the temperature difference between skin and air; a cooler skin means a smaller difference, so less heat is lost.
Predict what happens to core temperature if the volunteer stays for several hours. Explain.
It keeps falling slowly (hypothermia) if heat loss stays greater than heat production as the volunteer tires.
